doc.title: Loren Schoenberg interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2019

title: Museum visitors and the Basie exhibit opening with Mingus on bass
summary: Weekend volunteering, people like Marge Singleton and Harry Carney, and recording the Basie exhibit opening where Mingus took the bass.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: friends with Bobby Hackett and he was like an adopted son of Louis’s, of Louis Armstrong, and a lifelong disciple of his. And he wound up becoming the manager of this small little jazz museum. And he took me on as a volunteer. So every Saturday and Sunday I would take the bus — you could take a bus from suburban New Jersey into New York, it was easy, and my parents let me do it, unbelievable. And I wound up volunteering there for years. And this is where I got to know Marge Singleton, Zutty Singleton’s wife, it’s where I got to know Clarence Armstrong, who was Louis Armstrong’s, I guess he was a cousin, he was mentally challenged. In those days they used the word slow or retarded. I don’t know what the right term is. But he was kind of like a big child. And because Jack was so close with Louis and the family he would spend weekends there. A little bit later Duke Ellington was — we didn’t know but he was dying in the hospital so Harry Carney came in, and Harold Ashby used to come in and spend weekends just hanging around this jazz museum, so I got to know all these people. There was an opening of an exhibit on Count Basie and I brought my little — at that time I had a hand-held cassette machine that was about this big, you remember, that you press the button like this, and I remember bringing it in and I tape recorded on a cassette the first opening night. And it was Eddie Durham, Buddy Tate, Al Gray, Chuck Folds on piano, Eddie Jones on bass and Jo Jones on drums, and a few others who I got to know later. And Paul Quinichette was there. And then, who comes in but Basie. So Basie plays the piano. Then who muscles his way through the crowd — now Eddie Jones if you remember, I think you interviewed him.

Not the bassist. Eddie Jones was about six feet — he could have been a football player — like six foot six, big guy. Somebody comes and taps him on the shoulder and takes the bass. It’s Charles Mingus. And I recorded this on my little tape. I gave it to Phil Schaap, I never saw it again, but I’m just joking because Phil gave it back to me thirty years later.
